titel: Ed Conway: Why we won't run out of materials

faehigkeiten.grund: Dynamik weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen (Abruf laeuft ueber den Werbedienst omny.fm) - zu wenig fuer ein Urteil, aber nicht nichts

einzeiler: Ed Conway on why physical progress makes running out of raw materials a myth.
kurzfassung: Sky News editor Ed Conway discusses his bestselling book The Material World and challenges the narrative that humanity is running out of physical resources. He explains the hidden energy and material supply chains behind everyday items like tomatoes and data centers. The conversation also explores the psychology of zero-sum thinking, the role of public opinion, and the upcoming book Trade World.
stichpunkte: Ed Conway emphasizes how modern technological advances and physical progress are often taken for granted.
The production of everyday items like tomatoes relies heavily on complex energy inputs, synthetic fertilizers, and fossil fuels.
Despite popular fears, geological data shows no sign that humanity is running out of essential minerals like copper and lithium.
Zero-sum thinking and nostalgia bias drive public pessimism about resource scarcity and the future.
Technological innovations and productivity gains continually expand resource reserves rather than depleting them.
Data centers and AI infrastructure carry massive physical footprints, highlighting our ongoing dependence on heavy materials.
Public skepticism and political resistance pose the greatest hurdles to industrial projects and clean energy transitions.
Trade World explores the complex, global supply chains behind everyday goods such as bread, clothing, and cars.

clips.hook: A personal story of how antibiotics saved a life.
clips.text: The guest shares a personal family history involving tuberculosis and an early course of antibiotics that ultimately saved a life.
Copper reserves consistently increase over time as exploration techniques improve.

clips.hook: The main product of a blast furnace is carbon dioxide.
clips.text: Traditional steel-making blast furnaces produce a greater weight of carbon dioxide than actual iron.

clips.hook: More transistors in the world than leaves.
clips.text: Manufacturing capability has reached such heights that there are orders of magnitude more transistors than tree leaves.

clips.hook: Any amount of GDP is a form of energy conversion.
clips.text: Economic output is fundamentally tied to energy conversion, meaning higher energy costs drive up prices everywhere.

beschreibung:
From tomatoes and copper to data centers and steel, the modern economy depends on a material world hidden in plain sight.
In this episode of the Century of Plenty podcast, Sven Smit and Chris Bradley are joined by Ed Conway, economics and data editor at Sky News and author of Material World, to explore the materials, energy, infrastructure, and trade that underpin modern prosperity—and what it would take to extend it to everyone. They discuss:
◼ How the hidden material foundations of modern life—from fertilizer and steel to copper and semiconductors—make abundance possible, and why fears of simply “running out” of resources can miss the role of innovation, discovery, and productivity.
◼ Why achieving higher living standards around the world will require far more energy and physical infrastructure, and how abundant clean energy, intensive agriculture, and new approaches to manufacturing could reconcile development with climate goals.
◼ Why pessimism about the future persists despite centuries of progress—and how AI and a renewed focus on energy, infrastructure, and industry could strengthen the case for investing in abundance.
